title: Cross-cultural validation of the AAQ-II in five countries: A SEM and psychometric network analysis approaches
abstract: Background Experiential avoidance (EA) describes the tendency to evade negative internal experiences (e.g., distressing thoughts, emotions). EA is implicated across mental health conditions, positioning it as a central target for interventions like Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT). The Acceptance and Action Questionnaire-II (AAQ-II) is widely employed to measure EA; however, its cross-cultural reliability and factorial stability have not been comprehensively validated across diverse contexts. Aim This study aimed to assess the cross-cultural validity and psychometric stability of the AAQ-II across five countries (Peru, Mexico, USA, Belgium, and Hungary) using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and network analysis. Method A sample of 3,719 adults, primarily female (63.65%), was collected from five countries. Data analysis included SEM to evaluate factorial structure and network analysis to examine item interrelationships, assessing Expected Influence (EI) as a centrality measure. Multiverse analysis using 5,000 bootstrap samples further evaluated network stability across samples. Results SEM confirmed a unidimensional AAQ-II structure across all regions, indicating consistent factorial validity. Network analysis identified "Painful Memories" (AAQ4) and "Painful Experiences" (AAQ1) as central nodes across cultures, with regional variations in item relationships reflecting unique sociocultural influences. For instance, individualistic societies (e.g., USA) emphasized EA linked to achievement and competitive concerns, while collectivist countries (e.g., Peru, Mexico) associated EA with familial and social obligations. Multiverse analysis revealed stable EA constructs across samples. Discussion Results validate the cross-cultural applicability of the AAQ-II, with findings underscoring cultural impacts on EA manifestations. Network analysis provided nuanced insights into item interactions, showing that cultural factors, such as individualism, historical trauma, and social norms, shape EA expression differently across regions. This supports the use of culturally informed approaches in EA interventions. Conclusion The AAQ-II exhibits reliable cross-cultural validity, affirming its utility for assessing EA across diverse settings. These findings enhance the application of the tool in psychological therapies worldwide, suggesting that culturally tailored EA interventions may benefit from considering specific sociocultural factors influencing EA processes. Future research should investigate additional variables that may affect EA in different cultural contexts.
